newsitem.title: HONDURAS: Drug trade threatens disappearing Honduran Indians.
newsitem.headline: Drug trade threatens disappearing Honduran Indians.

text.p: Honduran Indians on the country's Caribbean coast said on Monday Colombian drug traffickers were buying up their ancestral lands and turning them into landing strips for use in the cocaine trade.
Tawahka Indians, whose number has dwindled to 900, are being forced off their lands and are asking the government to step in to halt the trend.
"They are moving us off the lands where we have always lived," Edgardo Benitez, a leader of the Tawahka Indians, told reporters. "Men come to cut down trees and a lot of them are armed."

Benitez said the future of the tribe also was threatened by farmers, cattle ranchers and loggers encroaching on their territory. "There are Colombians who are buying land on the Mosquito Coast, from where it is evident that they are launching drug trafficking," he said.

Honduran anti-drug officials have said they are investigating large land purchases by Colombian residents of Honduras in the area of Sico Paulaya in the Caribbean region known as the Mosquito Coast or Mosquitia. They also have said that drug traffickers operate several clandestine airstrips in the country.
"This drug trafficking in Mosquitia has been going on for many years," Benitez said. "Planes appear and then disappear in the middle of the mountains."

During a trial in Colombia, accused Cali cartel leader Miguel Rodriguez Orejuela testified that he participated in 32 drug shipments in Honduras and neighbouring Guatemala, according to Colombian press reports. Last week, Rodriguez was sentenced to nine years and fined $4.4 million after pleading guilty. He could walk free in five years.
